prompt_sources.name: Example: Identifying Pairs of Linearly Dependent and Linearly Independent Functions
prompt_sources.problem: Given the set of functions $\{ e^x, \, \sin x \}$ defined on $x \in \mathbb{R},$ explain why they are linearly independent.
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
Recall that the set of functions $\{ f_1(x), f_2(x), \ldots, f_n(x) \},$ which are defined on some interval $I,$ is *linearly dependent* if there exist real scalars $k_1,k_2,\ldots,k_n$ not all zero such that the linear combination $k_1 \cdot f_1 + k_2 \cdot f_2 + \ldots + k_2 \cdot f_2$ is identically zero, i.e, 

$$
k_1 \cdot f_1(x) + k_2 \cdot f_2(x) + \ldots + k_2 \cdot f_2(x) = 0
$$

for all $x \in I.$ Otherwise, if $k_1 = k_2 = \cdots = k_n = 0$ is the only solution, the set is *linearly independent*.

Now, suppose for all $x \in \mathbb{R},$ we have that 

$$
k_1 e^x + k_2 \sin x = 0.
$$

For example:

- If $x=0,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & {k}_{1}({e}^{0})+{k}_{2}(\operatorname{sin} 0)=0 \\  & {k}_{1}\cdot 1+{k}_{2}\cdot 0=0\,⇒\,{k}_{1}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=1,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned} & {k}_{1}({e}^{1})+{k}_{2}(\operatorname{sin} 1)=0 \\  & e{k}_{1}+(\operatorname{sin} 1)\,{k}_{2}=0\,⇒\,e{k}_{1}+(\operatorname{sin} 1)\,{k}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\begin{cases}{k}_{1}=0 \\ e{k}_{1}+(\operatorname{sin} 1)\,{k}_{2}=0\end{cases}
$$

The only solution for this system is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{k_1=k_2=0}.$

Therefore, since $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{all}}$ the scalar coefficients in the linear combination must be zero, the given set of functions is linearly $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{independent}}.$

Recall that the set of functions $\{{f}_{1}(x),{f}_{2}(x),…,{f}_{n}(x)\},$ which are defined on some interval $I,$ is *linearly dependent* if there exist real scalars ${k}_{1},{k}_{2},…,{k}_{n}$ not all zero such that the linear combination ${k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}$ is identically zero, i.e, 

$$
{k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}(x)+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}(x)+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}(x)=0
$$

for all $x\in I.$ Otherwise, if ${k}_{1}={k}_{2}=⋯={k}_{n}=0$ is the only solution, the set is *linearly independent*.

Now, for all $x\in \mathbb{R},$ we have that 

$$
2\cdot x+0\cdot {e}^{x}+(-1)\cdot 2x=0.
$$

Therefore, since $\text{not all}$ the scalar coefficients in the linear combination are zero, the given set of functions is linearly $\text{dependent}.$

prompt_sources.name: Question 1
prompt_sources.problem:
Given the set of functions $\{\,7\operatorname{sin} x,\,5\operatorname{cos} x,\,-5\operatorname{cos} x\}$ defined on $x\in \mathbb{R},$ select the correct options in the following reasoning. For all $x\in \mathbb{R},$  we have that

$$
{{field-1}}\cdot 7\operatorname{sin} x\,+\,{{field-2}}\cdot 5\operatorname{cos} x\,+\,{{field-3}}\cdot (-5\operatorname{cos} x)=0.
$$

Since 
{{field-4}} 
the scalar coefficients in the linear combination are zero, the given set of functions is linearly 
{{field-5}}.

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Recall that the set of functions $\{{f}_{1}(x),{f}_{2}(x),…,{f}_{n}(x)\},$ which are defined on some interval $I,$ is *linearly dependent* if there exist real scalars ${k}_{1},{k}_{2},…,{k}_{n}$ not all zero such that the linear combination ${k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}$ is identically zero, i.e, 

$$
{k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}(x)+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}(x)+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}(x)=0
$$

for all $x\in I.$ Otherwise, if ${k}_{1}={k}_{2}=⋯={k}_{n}=0$ is the only solution, the set is *linearly independent*.

Now, for all $x\in \mathbb{R},$ we have that 

$$
0\cdot 7\operatorname{sin} x\,+\,4\cdot 5\operatorname{cos} x\,+\,4\cdot (-5\operatorname{cos} x)=0.
$$

Therefore, since $\text{not all}$ the scalar coefficients in the linear combination are zero, the given set of functions is linearly $\text{dependent}.$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Recall that the set of functions $\{{f}_{1}(x),{f}_{2}(x),…,{f}_{n}(x)\},$ which are defined on some interval $I,$ is *linearly dependent* if there exist real scalars ${k}_{1},{k}_{2},…,{k}_{n}$ not all zero such that the linear combination ${k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}$ is identically zero, i.e, 

$$
{k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}(x)+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}(x)+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}(x)=0
$$

for all $x\in I.$ Otherwise, if ${k}_{1}={k}_{2}=⋯={k}_{n}=0$ is the only solution, the set is *linearly independent*.

Now, for all $x\in \mathbb{R},$ we have that 

$$
3\cdot \operatorname{sin} x+0\cdot {e}^{x}+(-1)\cdot 3\operatorname{sin} x=0.
$$

  

Therefore, since $\text{not all}$ the scalar coefficients in the linear combination are zero, the given set of functions is linearly $\text{dependent}.$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Recall that the set of functions $\{{f}_{1}(x),{f}_{2}(x),…,{f}_{n}(x)\},$ which are defined on some interval $I,$ is *linearly dependent* if there exist real scalars ${k}_{1},{k}_{2},…,{k}_{n}$ not all zero such that the linear combination ${k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}$ is identically zero, i.e, 

$$
{k}_{1}\cdot {f}_{1}(x)+{k}_{2}\cdot {f}_{2}(x)+…+{k}_{n}\cdot {f}_{n}(x)=0
$$

for all $x\in I.$ Otherwise, if ${k}_{1}={k}_{2}=⋯={k}_{n}=0$ is the only solution, the set is *linearly independent*.

Now, suppose for all $x\in \mathbb{R},$ we have that 

$$
{k}_{1}{e}^{x}+{k}_{2}x=0.
$$

For example:

- If $x=0,$ we get 

$$
{k}_{1}({e}^{0})+{k}_{2}(0)=0\,⇒\,{k}_{1}=0.
$$

- If $x=\operatorname{ln} 2,$ we get 

$$
{k}_{1}({e}^{\operatorname{ln} 2})+{k}_{2}(\operatorname{ln} 2)=0\,⇒\,2{k}_{1}+(\operatorname{ln} 2){k}_{2}=0.
$$

Thus, we obtain the following system of linear equations:

$$
\begin{cases}{k}_{1}=0 \\ 2{k}_{1}+(\operatorname{ln} 2){k}_{2}=0\end{cases}
$$

The only solution for this system is ${k}_{1}={k}_{2}=0.$

Therefore, since $\text{all}$ the scalar coefficients in the linear combination must be zero, the given set of functions is linearly $\text{independent}.$

prompt_sources.name: Example: Calculating the Wronskian of Two Functions
prompt_sources.problem: Compute the Wronskian $W(y_1, y_2)$ for $y_1(x) =2x$ and $y_2(x) = x^2.$
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W(y_1,y_2)$ of two functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ is defined as

![](@asset-0@)

In our case, we have $y_1(x) = 2x$ and $y_2(x) = x^2.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =2x{({x}^{2})}^{′}-{x}^{2}{(2x)}^{′} \\  & =4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{2} \\  & =2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of two functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

In our case, we have ${y}_{1}(x)=x$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin} x.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =(x){(\operatorname{sin} x)}^{′}-(\operatorname{sin} x){(x)}^{′} \\  & =(x)(\operatorname{cos} x)-(\operatorname{sin} x)(1) \\  & =x\operatorname{cos} x-\operatorname{sin} x.\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of two functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

In our case, we have ${y}_{1}(x)=x$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=x\operatorname{sin} x.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =(x){(x\operatorname{sin} x)}^{′}-(x\operatorname{sin} x){(x)}^{′} \\  & =x(\operatorname{sin} x+x\operatorname{cos} x)-(x\operatorname{sin} x)(1) \\  & =x\operatorname{sin} x+{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos} x-x\operatorname{sin} x \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{cos} x\end{aligned}
$$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of two functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ is defined as:

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}
$$

In our case, we have ${y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos} (2x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin} (2x).$ Therefore:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =(\operatorname{cos} (2x)){(\operatorname{sin} (2x))}^{′}-(\operatorname{sin} (2x)){(\operatorname{cos} (2x))}^{′} \\  & =(\operatorname{cos} (2x))(2\operatorname{cos} (2x))-(\operatorname{sin} (2x))(-2\operatorname{sin} (2x)) \\  & =2{\operatorname{cos} }^{2}(2x)+2{\operatorname{sin} }^{2}(2x) \\  & =2({\operatorname{cos} }^{2}(2x)+{\operatorname{sin} }^{2}(2x)) \\  & =2(1) \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

prompt_sources.problem: Compute the Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ for ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos} x.$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of two functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

In our case, we have ${y}_{1}(x)={e}^{x}$ and ${y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{cos} x.$ Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =({e}^{x}){(\operatorname{cos} x)}^{′}-(\operatorname{cos} x){({e}^{x})}^{′} \\  & =({e}^{x})(-\operatorname{sin} x)-(\operatorname{cos} x)({e}^{x}) \\  & =-{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin} x-{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos} x \\  & =-{e}^{x}(\operatorname{sin} x+\operatorname{cos} x).\end{aligned}
$$

prompt_sources.name: Example: Identifying Pairs of Linearly Independent Functions Using the Wronskian
prompt_sources.problem:
$$
y_1(x) = x^2 + 1, \qquad
y_2(x) = 2x, \qquad x \in \mathbb R
$$

Consider the functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ above. Given that $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of the same second-order linear differential equation, use the Wronskian to explain why the set $\{ y_1(x), y_2(x) \}$ is linearly independent.
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
Suppose the functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ are defined on some interval $I.$
The Wronskian $W(y_1,y_2)$ of these functions is defined as
![](@asset-0@)

Recall the following:

- If $W \neq 0$ for at least one $x \in I,$ then $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly independent.

- If $W = 0$ and it’s known that $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then $y_1$ and $y_2$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & 2x \\ ({x}^{2}+1)^{′} & (2x)^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & 2x \\ 2x & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)\cdot 2-(2x)\cdot (2x) \\  & =2({x}^{2}+1)-4{x}^{2} \\  & =2{x}^{2}+2-4{x}^{2} \\  & =2-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

which is nonzero for at least one $x \in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\left\{ y_1(x), y_2(x) \right\}$ is linearly independent on $\mathbb R.$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Suppose the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are defined on some interval $I.$
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

Recall the following:

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If $W=0$ and it’s known that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x+1} & {e}^{2x} \\ {({e}^{2x+1})}^{′} & {({e}^{2x})}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x+1} & {e}^{2x} \\ 2{e}^{2x+1} & 2{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{2x+1}\cdot 2{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{2x+1} \\  & =2{e}^{4x+1}-2{e}^{4x+1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is $\text{zero for all }x\in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{dependent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

Suppose the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are defined on some interval $I.$
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

Recall the following:

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If $W=0$ and it’s known that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & 2+2{x}^{2} \\ ({x}^{2}+1)^{′} & (2+2{x}^{2})^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+1 & 2+2{x}^{2} \\ 2x & 4x\end{aligned}| \\  & =({x}^{2}+1)(4x)-(2+2{x}^{2})(2x) \\  & =4x({x}^{2}+1)-4x({x}^{2}+1) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is $\text{zero for all }x\in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{dependent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}x+1 & {x}^{2} \\ (x+1)^{′} & ({x}^{2})^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}x+1 & {x}^{2} \\ 1 & 2x\end{aligned}| \\  & =(x+1)\cdot (2x)-{x}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =2x(x+1)-{x}^{2} \\  & =2{x}^{2}+2x-{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+2x \\  & =x(x+2)\end{aligned}

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{independent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

$$

which is $\text{nonzero for at least one }x\in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{independent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

Recall the following:

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If $W=0$ and it’s known that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & {e}^{2x} \\ ({e}^{x})^{′} & ({e}^{2x})^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{x} & {e}^{2x} \\ {e}^{x} & 2{e}^{2x}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{x}\cdot 2{e}^{2x}-{e}^{2x}\cdot {e}^{x} \\  & =2{e}^{3x}-{e}^{3x} \\  & ={e}^{3x}\end{aligned}
$$

which is $\text{nonzero for at least one }x\in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{independent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

Suppose the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are defined on some interval $I.$
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

Recall the following:

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If $W=0$ and it’s known that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2x & 10x-5{x}^{3} \\ ({x}^{3}-2x)^{′} & (10x-5{x}^{3})^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}-2x & 10x-5{x}^{3} \\ 3{x}^{2}-2 & 10-15{x}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =({x}^{3}-2x)(10-15{x}^{2})-(10x-5{x}^{3})(3{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =x({x}^{2}-2)\cdot 5(2-3{x}^{2})-5x(2-{x}^{2})(3{x}^{2}-2) \\  & =5x({x}^{2}-2)(2-3{x}^{2})-5x({x}^{2}-2)(2-3{x}^{2}) \\  & =-15{x}^{5}+40{x}^{3}-20x-(-15{x}^{5}+40{x}^{3}-20x) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is $\text{zero for all }x\in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{dependent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

Suppose the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are defined on some interval $I.$
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

Recall the following:

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If $W=0$ and it’s known that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin} x & \operatorname{cos} x+1 \\ {(\operatorname{sin} x)}^{′} & {(\operatorname{cos} x+1)}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin} x & \operatorname{cos} x+1 \\ \operatorname{cos} x & -\operatorname{sin} x\end{aligned}| \\  & =\operatorname{sin} x\cdot (-\operatorname{sin} x)-(\operatorname{cos} x+1)\cdot \operatorname{cos} x \\  & =-{\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x-({\operatorname{cos} }^{2}x+\operatorname{cos} x) \\  & =-({\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x+{\operatorname{cos} }^{2}x)-\operatorname{cos} x \\  & =-1-\operatorname{cos} x\end{aligned}
$$

which is $\text{nonzero for at least one }x\in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{independent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

solution_sources.worked_solution:
Suppose the functions ${y}_{1}(x)$ and ${y}_{2}(x)$ are defined on some interval $I.$
The Wronskian $W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})$ of these functions is defined as

$$
W({y}_{1},{y}_{2})=|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}|={y}_{1}{y}_{2}^{′}-{y}_{2}{y}_{1}^{′}.
$$

Recall the following:

- If $W\ne 0$ for at least one $x\in I,$ then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly independent.

- If $W=0$ and it’s known that ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are solutions to the same second-order linear differential equation, then ${y}_{1}$ and ${y}_{2}$ are linearly dependent.

In our case, the Wronskian is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}2{\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x & 1-{\operatorname{cos} }^{2}x \\ {(2{\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x)}^{′} & {(1-{\operatorname{cos} }^{2}x)}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2{\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x & 1-{\operatorname{cos} }^{2}x \\ 4\operatorname{sin} x\operatorname{cos} x & 2\operatorname{sin} x\operatorname{cos} x\end{aligned}| \\  & =(2{\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x)(2\operatorname{sin} x\operatorname{cos} x)-(1-{\operatorname{cos} }^{2}x)(4\operatorname{sin} x\operatorname{cos} x) \\  & =4({\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x)(\operatorname{sin} x\operatorname{cos} x)-4({\operatorname{sin} }^{2}x)(\operatorname{sin} x\operatorname{cos} x) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

which is $\text{zero for all }x\in \mathbb{R}.$

Therefore, the set $\{{y}_{1}(x),{y}_{2}(x)\}$ is linearly $\text{dependent}$ on $\mathbb{R}.$

prompt_sources.name: Example: Identifying Fundamental Sets of Solutions
prompt_sources.problem:
Consider the differential equation $x^2y'' - 5x y' + 9y=0.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $y_1(x) = x^3$ is a solution to the equation for $x\in \mathbb R.$

II. $y_2(x) = x^3 \ln x$ is a solution to the equation for $x > 0.$

III. The functions $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0, \infty).$
prompt_sources.worked_solution:
Recall that to determine whether $y(x)$ is a solution to the differential equation, we substitute $y$ and its derivatives into the equation. 

Let's check each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of $y_1(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{″}(x) & =6x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute $y_1(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot 6x-5x\cdot 3{x}^{2}+9{x}^{3} & =0 \\ 6{x}^{3}-15{x}^{3}+9{x}^{3} & =0 \\ 0 & =0{\color{darkgreen}\,✓}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y_1(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement II is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of $y_2(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln} x+{x}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =6x\operatorname{ln} x+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute $y_2(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}(6x\operatorname{ln} x+5x)-5x(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln} x+{x}^{2})+9{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln} x & =0 \\ (6{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln} x+5{x}^{3}-15{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln} x-5{x}^{3}+9{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln} x) & =0 \\ 0 & =0{\color{darkgreen}\,✓}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y_2(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement III is true. Both $y_1$ and $y_2$ are solutions of the equation. To check if these functions are linearly independent, we compute the Wronskian:

$$
\begin{aligned}W({y}_{1},{y}_{2}) & =|\begin{aligned}{y}_{1} & {y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{′} & {y}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{x}^{3} & {x}^{3}\operatorname{ln} x \\ 3{x}^{2} & 3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln} x+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & ={x}^{3}(3{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln} x+{x}^{2})-{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln} x\cdot 3{x}^{2} \\  & =3{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln} x+{x}^{5}-3{x}^{5}\operatorname{ln} x \\  & ={x}^{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the  Wronskian is not identically $0$ on $(0, \infty),$ the functions are linearly independent. Hence, $y_1(x)$ and $y_2(x)$ form a set of fundamental solutions to the equation on $(0, \infty)$.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

$$

$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{1}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\operatorname{sin} (x)+\operatorname{sin} (x) & =0 \\ 0 & =0{\color{darkgreen}\,✓}\end{aligned}
$$

So, ${y}_{1}(x)$ is a solution to the equation.

- Statement II is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}^{′}(x) & =3\operatorname{cos} (x) \\ {y}_{2}^{″}(x) & =-3\operatorname{sin} (x)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's substitute ${y}_{2}(x)$ and its derivatives into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\operatorname{sin} (x)+3\operatorname{sin} (x) & =0 \\ 0 & =0{\color{darkgreen}\,✓}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

- Statement II is true. First, we find the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{2}(x).$ Notice that $\sqrt{x}={x}^{\frac{1}{2}},$ so we have:

$$
